nameStory: The twig pruner gets its name from its unusual lifecycle habit of literally pruning tree branches! The larva (baby beetle) chews a neat circle around a twig from the inside, weakening it so the wind breaks it off with the larva still inside, dropping safely to the ground to continue developing.
description: The twig pruner is a medium-sized longhorn beetle with a brownish body covered in fine, fuzzy hairs that give it a somewhat velvety appearance. Like all longhorn beetles, it has notably long antennae that can be as long as or longer than its body. Adults are typically around half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, with a cylindrical body shape typical of wood-boring beetles.

idTips.label: Fuzzy brown body
idTips.description: The entire beetle has a soft, velvety texture due to dense, fine hairs covering its brownish body - run your finger gently over it and it feels almost like suede

idTips.label: Extra-long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are distinctly longer than the body length, segmented like beads on a string, and constantly moving as the beetle explores

idTips.label: Cylindrical body shape
idTips.description: Body is tube-like and elongated rather than flattened, fitting the wood-boring lifestyle of tunneling through branches

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: About the length of your thumbnail, substantial enough to notice but not as large as some of the giant longhorns

idTips.label: Strong, sturdy legs
idTips.description: Legs are thick and powerful for gripping bark and wood surfaces, with tiny claws that you can feel if one walks across your hand

habitat: Found in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly where oak, maple, hickory, and other hardwood trees are present. Look for them on or near dead or dying branches, fallen logs, and woodpiles from sea level to moderate elevations in the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from overwintered pupae in dead wood. You might find fresh exit holes in fallen branches or see adults beginning to move around on warm days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, mating and laying eggs in weakened or dead branches. This is when you're most likely to spot them crawling on tree bark or flying to lights at night.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down, but this is prime time to find the evidence of their work - freshly cut twigs and small branches littering the forest floor beneath trees.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off, but larvae are actively feeding inside fallen branches on the ground, slowly chewing their characteristic circular cuts that will drop the twigs next year.

funFact: Twig pruner larvae are nature's tiny lumberjacks - they can precisely calculate exactly how much wood to chew away so that their branch breaks off in the next strong wind, but not before they've finished eating enough to survive the fall!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other brown longhorn beetles, but the twig pruner's distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture sets it apart from the shinier, smoother surfaces of most relatives. Remember: "Fuzzy pruner, smooth others."
contextualKnowledge: Scientists once thought there were two separate species - Anelaphus villosus and Anelaphus parallelus - but modern research has shown they're actually the same beetle, just with some natural variation in appearance.
compareHints: Since this is the only Anelaphus species in New England, compare it to other longhorn beetles by its signature fuzzy texture and medium size. Most other longhorns in the region are either much larger with smooth, shiny bodies, or smaller and more colorful, lacking the twig pruner's distinctive velvety brown coat.
